claims.text: The initial alloy is a non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution containing the full HEA mixture.
Mg atoms are initially evenly distributed throughout the alloy.
The initial state contains no significant intermetallic compounds.
Exposure at 400–600°C accelerates atomic diffusion and aging relative to the initial state.
Diffusion enables local compositional segregation and the nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic phases.
The transformation follows a diffusion-limited pathway.
Formation of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds reduces the alloy's overall entropy stabilization.
Mg-rich intermetallic formation produces a heterogeneous microstructure that forms micro-galvanic cells.
The heterogeneous intermetallic-containing microstructure compromises the integrity and uniformity of protective oxide or passive films.
Compromising the protective films diminishes corrosion resistance.
Compromising the protective films diminishes high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Aged specimens will contain distinct Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates detectable by microscopy and phase analysis.
Aged specimens will have lower corrosion resistance than the initial metastable state.
Aged specimens will have poorer high-temperature oxidation performance than the initial metastable state.
The metastable as-cast or rapidly solidified baseline has high corrosion resistance.
The metastable as-cast or rapidly solidified baseline has high oxidation resistance.
Approximately 400–600°C is the relevant service-regime boundary at which atomic mobility becomes sufficient to trigger the proposed transformation.
The 400–600°C regime remains below temperatures causing complete melting or catastrophic failure.
The precise nucleation and growth kinetics and their quantitative effects on corrosion and oxidation remain undetermined.
